Nineteen Hours, Two of Them Running

Hood to Coast 2019, as remembered by my watch

I ran Hood to Coast once. When I sat down to write about it, I couldn’t have told you whether it was 2018 or 2019.

My watch had no such trouble. Friday, August 23, 2019, 7:45 in the evening, Gresham, Oregon: an activity called “Evening Run.” It is followed by a “Morning Run” at 5:15 the next day and an “Afternoon Run” at 1:59. Strava had no idea I was in a race.Other runners did. Each of the three runs crosses a Strava segment that somebody named after the relay: “Leg 10 HTC,” “Leg 22 HTC,” “HTC Leg 34.” That is how I know which legs were mine.

Hood to Coast is a relay of about {{course}} miles, from Timberline Lodge on Mount Hood to the beach at Seaside. It is cut into 36 legs and shared by twelve people in two vans, and each runner takes three legs. Legs 10, 22 and 34 make me runner ten, in the second van. I wanted to see what the watch had kept that I hadn’t.

Three marks on a map

Drawn to scale, my share of the race is three short marks: {{run_mi:.1f}} miles of {{course}}, or about {{share:.0f}} percent. Runner ten doesn’t start on the mountain and doesn’t finish on the beach. The first leg follows the Springwater Trail west through Gresham, the second goes over Apiary Road in the hills of Columbia County, and the third ends about two legs short of the ocean.

Mostly, you wait

From the first step of my first leg to the last step of my third, {{span}} went by. I was running for {{run_time}} of it, which is {{run_pct:.0f}} percent. The other {{off}} happened in a van, and the watch has nothing to say about them.

It does know what the light was doing. The first leg started {{before_sunset}} minutes before sunset and finished at {{end10}}, in the dusk. The second started more than an hour before sunrise. Only the third was run in full daylight, after a second wait of {{gap2}}.

Faster on no sleep

Here is what I expected the numbers to show: a decent first leg, a grim one in the dark, and a shuffle to the finish. That is how a night in a van is supposed to go.

{{rows}}
The three legs, from my watch
StartMilesTimePaceBest mileBest 5KClimb, ft

Oddly though, it went the other way. I ran {{p10}} a mile on Friday evening, {{p22}} before dawn, and {{p34}} on Saturday afternoon, eighteen hours in. Each leg was faster than the one before it.

Why would this be the case? The obvious suspect is the ground.

All three legs share one pace scale, one elevation scale and one distance scale, so a mile is the same width in each panel. Pace is smoothed over about a quarter mile and skips the first fifth of a mile, where the GPS is still finding itself. The dotted line is the average for the leg.The ground explains the middle leg and not much else. Leg 22 opens with a climb of {{climb_ft:.0f}} feet in {{climb_mi:.1f}} miles, which I ran at {{climb_pace}} a mile in the dark. Then the road drops {{drop_ft:.0f}} feet over the next {{drop_mi:.1f}} miles and I ran those at {{drop_pace}}. That leg was fast because most of it was downhill.

The other two have no such excuse. Leg 10 loses {{drop10:.0f}} feet in five and a half miles, which is to say it is flat, and it was my slowest. Leg 34 rolls over a few small hills, finishes {{net34:.0f}} feet higher than it starts, and was my fastest.

Leg 34 was also the shortest, and short runs are quicker. So compare like with like. The fastest 5K inside each leg was {{k10}}, then {{k22}}, then {{k34}}. The fastest mile was {{m10}}, then {{m22}}, then {{m34}}. The order doesn’t change.

The watch can’t take it further than that. It recorded no heart rate, so it doesn’t know how hard any of this felt. It would be reasonable to assume that some of it was daylight, some of it was knowing this was the last one, and some of it was eleven people waiting at the next exchange.

Ten days of evidence

The log holds a second surprise. After a bike ride in April 2017 it is empty for more than two years. Then, on August 13, 2019, there is a run. Four more follow within the week.Either I trained for a {{course}}-mile relay in {{train_days}} days, or I started recording {{lead_days}} days before it. I would like to believe the second. The log can’t settle it.

Every run Strava has from me in 2019, in order, evenly spaced. Faster is higher. Hover over a dot for the details.That is the whole build-up on record: {{train_n}} runs, {{train_mi:.1f}} miles, at an average of {{train_pace}} a mile. The quickest of them was {{train_best}}. My slowest leg of the relay was {{race_worst}}. Every leg of the race was faster than every run that came before it, and the three together averaged {{race_pace}}, which is {{faster}} seconds a mile quicker than the training.

Then it stops. There is one run in September and two in December. The year comes to {{year_n}} runs and {{year_mi:.0f}} miles, and three of the runs happened inside nineteen hours.

What it cost later

Here’s the uncomfortable part. Last year I trained for 22 weeks to run the Dallas Half Marathon, and wrote about it at some length. I ran it at {{half}} a mile. In 2019, on ten days of logged running and a night in a van, I averaged {{race_pace}} over {{run_mi:.1f}} miles.

The comparison flatters 2019. A half marathon is 13.1 miles without stopping, and the relay gave me two breaks of about eight hours. Still, my best 5K in all of 2025 was {{k2025}}. The one inside leg 34, run on a Saturday afternoon after two earlier legs and no bed, was {{k34}}. That is {{kgap}} seconds slower.

I was also six years younger.

What the watch kept

The watch kept the date, the pace and the hills. It lost the van, the other eleven runners and whatever we ate at four in the morning. Between the two of us we have most of it.

It was 2019.
